full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractEmerging and re-emerging infectious diseases continue to pose a persistent challenge to global public health security. As an unbiased and noninvasive population-level surveillance approach, wastewater-based epidemiology has emerged as an urban-scale monitoring tool for proactively capturing the community disease burden. In this study, metagenomic and targeted next-generation sequencing were employed to preliminarily characterize wastewater viral communities in Gansu Province from 2024 to 2026. Across the three annual sampling groups, the Simpson diversity index calculated from metagenomic taxonomic profiles showed a significant negative correlation with sampling year. Despite viral enrichment, more than 97% of sequencing reads were assigned to bacteria, likely reflecting residual nonviral nucleic acids and limitations in metagenomic classification. The wastewater virome exhibited a complex host-association spectrum, within which bacteriophages and plant-associated viruses displayed relatively stable community structures and high relative abundances. Among human pathogens, astroviruses were consistently detected at high relative abundances across all samples. Human astrovirus 1 accounted for the largest proportion, and a nearly complete genome sequence of the extraintestinal infection-associated astrovirus MLB2 was recovered. Targeted sequencing further revealed a highly structured environmental enterovirus profile dominated by the species Enterovirus betacoxsackie, followed by Enterovirus alphacoxsackie, whereas Enterovirus coxsackiepol was detected at an extremely low abundance and Enterovirus deconjuncti was not detected. In addition to several common viruses associated with hand, foot, and mouth disease, rare viruses, including coxsackievirus A19 and enterovirus B83, were successfully captured. Echovirus 11 was identified as the predominant enterovirus serotype in current wastewater surveillance in Gansu Province. In summary, this study provides a preliminary characterization of the viral community profiles in wastewater samples from Gansu Province, demonstrates the effectiveness of wastewater-based epidemiology for population-level surveillance, and underscores the need to establish a coordinated defense network integrating clinical case surveillance with environmental monitoring.Keywords: astroviruses, enterovirus, Gansu Province, metagenomic sequencing, targeted next-generation sequencing, wastewater
full_text_sections.methods: Materials and methodsCollection and processing of the wastewater samplesBetween 2024 and 2026, 18 raw wastewater samples were collected from wastewater treatment plants across 6 cities in Gansu Province (Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Dingxi). Based on their respective sampling years, the samples were categorized into 3 groups: GS24, GS25, and GS26. Seasonal patterns, population differences, and other demographic factors were not considered when defining these groups. Specifically, the sample groups were designated as follows: GS24-1 to GS24-6 were collected in July 2024 from Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Hezuo, respectively; GS25-1 to GS25-6 were collected in June 2025 from Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Zhangye, respectively; and GS26-1 to GS26-6 were collected in March 2026 from Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Dingxi, respectively. GS24-1 and GS24-6 were independently collected on the same day from the same wastewater treatment plant in Hezuo. The same applied to GS25-2 and GS25-6 in Zhangye. The collection dates reflected operational availability and were not selected to provide seasonally matched observations. At each monitoring site, 1 L of raw wastewater was collected. The samples were transported at 4 °C to the laboratory of Gansu Provincial Center for Disease Control and Prevention within 7 days and processed immediately upon arrival (Wang et al., 2014). For viral concentration, the wastewater samples were initially centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 30 min at 4 °C. Subsequently, 2.5 M MgCl2 was added to the supernatant to achieve a final concentration of 0.05 M, and the pH was adjusted to 3.5 using 0.5 N HCl. The prepared solution was then filtered through a 142-mm cellulose nitrate membrane using a positive-pressure pump. Following filtration, the membrane was fragmented and eluted twice with 10 mL of 3% beef extract by vortexing on ice for 5 min each time. The pooled eluates were centrifuged at 1,000 × g for 15 min at 4 °C and finally passed through a 0.22 μm syringe filter.Nucleic acid extraction and sequencingTotal nucleic acid extraction was performed using the High Pure Viral Nucleic Acid Kit (Roche) without DNase digestion. To reduce potential false-positive results associated with the increased PCR cycles required for capture-based sequencing, the initial extract was divided for parallel and independent library preparations. Metagenomic libraries were generated with the MGIEasy Fast RNA Library Prep Set, whereas the IGT® Fast Stranded RNA Library Prep Kit v2.0 was applied for capture-based construction. For targeted enrichment, a custom enterovirus probe panel was deployed; this panel was specifically designed for selected viruses, encompassing the species Enterovirus alphacoxsackie, Enterovirus betacoxsackie, Enterovirus coxsackiepol, and Enterovirus deconjuncti. Negative controls were processed in parallel during nucleic acid extraction and library preparation to monitor potential contamination, and no evidence of contamination or other procedural abnormalities was observed. Finally, paired-end reads were generated by sequencing the prepared libraries on a DNBSEQ-T7 platform.Sequence data analysisRaw sequencing reads generated by the metagenomic and targeted-capture workflows were assessed using FastQC1 before downstream analysis. No sequencing dataset was excluded from downstream analysis solely on the basis of the FastQC assessment. For raw paired-end reads, adapter trimming and quality filtering (length <50 bp, quality score <20, or containing N bases) were performed using KneadData.2 High-quality reads were then aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) via Bowtie2 to discard host sequences, with the unmapped reads kept for subsequent analyses (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012). Metagenomic reads were taxonomically classified using Kraken2 across multiple taxonomic levels (Wood et al., 2019). All sequencing reads were assembled using MEGAHIT (Li et al., 2015). Contigs (length ≥300 bp, coverage ≥3×) were filtered via awk and annotated using blastn, taking the highest bitscore as the final assignment (Chen et al., 2015). Read abundances per viral species were quantified using BWA-backtrack for downstream evaluation (Li and Durbin, 2009). All astrovirus- and enterovirus-associated contigs assembled using MEGAHIT were extracted from each sample and individually re-evaluated using NCBI BLASTn.3Rarefaction analysis and diversity visualizationAll statistical analyses and data visualizations were performed using R 4.4.3 software.4 Specifically, alpha diversity was assessed at the genus level, and the Shannon and inverse Simpson indices were calculated using the vegan package. Hereafter, the term “Simpson index” refers specifically to the inverse Simpson formulation (1/D). Temporal trends in alpha diversity were assessed using one-tailed Spearman’s rank correlation tests, with the a priori hypothesis that diversity indices would decline over sampling years. Spearman’s rho (ρ) values and corresponding one-sided p values were calculated to evaluate the monotonic relationship between sampling year and alpha diversity indices. Rarefaction curves, heatmaps, stacked bar plots, and visualizations of alpha diversity indices were generated using the ggplot2 package.Quantitative profiling of the viromeFor the quantitative analysis of viral communities, relative abundances were estimated using the reads per million normalization method described in Equation 1. The mapped read counts of each viral contig were adjusted for genome length differences by dividing the read counts by the average genome size of the corresponding viral family or genus. Subsequently, the adjusted read counts were normalized against the total number of reads assigned to all viral families or genera within each individual sample (Worp et al., 2025). This normalization strategy was consistently applied to all heatmaps generated in this study.However, a modified approach was applied for the stacked bar charts illustrating the relative abundances of different species within the genus Enterovirus. Because genome lengths among enterovirus serotypes are highly conserved, with an average size of approximately 7.4 kb, genome length normalization was omitted when calculating the relative abundance of enterovirus-associated contigs.(1)Relative abundance=virus readsaverage genome length×total viral reads×106The host type classifications for the viral families listed herein were retrieved from the Virus-Host Database.5Comparison of viral diversityTo compare viral community structure across sample groups, principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on centered log-ratio transformed abundance data (Gloor et al., 2017). Zero counts in the abundance matrices were replaced with a pseudocount equivalent to half of the minimum positive abundance value detected within the respective dataset, as centered log-ratio transformation requires strictly positive values. Viral taxa contributing most strongly to the principal components were identified based on the magnitude of their loadings. PCA biplots were generated using the ggplot2 package in R 4.4.3 software, with 68% confidence ellipses overlaid to visualize group clustering.Phylogenetic analysisReference viral VP1 gene sequences were retrieved from GenBank at the National Center for biotechnology information (NCBI). These sequences, together with the VP1 sequences generated in this study, were aligned using MAFFT v7.520 (Katoh and Standley, 2013). Neighbor-joining (NJ) phylogenetic trees were constructed in MEGA7 based on evolutionary distances calculated using the maximum composite likelihood method (Kumar et al., 2016). The robustness of the inferred tree topologies was assessed by bootstrap analysis with 1,000 replicates (Felsenstein, 1985), and bootstrap support values of 70% or higher were displayed at the corresponding nodes. full_text_sections.results: ResultsBetween-year variation in alpha diversity and broad taxonomic compositionRarefaction analysis showed that the sequencing captured most of the detectable genus-level diversity across the three sampling groups, indicating that the sequencing depth was sufficient (Figure 1A). Overall metagenomic sequencing statistics and alpha diversity indices (including the Shannon and Simpson indices) are summarized in Table 1 and visualized in Figures 1B,C. Sampling year was treated as an ordinal variable. The Shannon index showed a negative but nonsignificant correlation with sampling year (Spearman’s ρ = −0.354, p = 0.075). In contrast, the Simpson index exhibited a significant negative correlation with sampling year (Spearman’s ρ = −0.472, p = 0.024). Given that the dataset comprised only three annual sampling campaigns conducted in different months, these analyses were considered exploratory assessments of between-year variation. At the broadest taxonomic level, more than 97% of reads in each dataset were assigned to Bacteria, whereas no more than 0.94% were classified as viral (Table 2). Following taxonomic classification with Kraken2, 56.42–74.74% of the metagenomic reads across samples remained unclassified at the genus level (Supplementary Table S1). In this context, “unclassified” indicates that the reference database and parameter settings did not provide sufficient evidence for a reliable taxonomic assignment. The unclassified reads were not subjected to further characterization in this study.Figure 1Overview of metagenomic sequencing data across the three groups. (A) Rarefaction curves at the genus level. (B) Shannon index. (C) Simpson index.Panel A shows rarefaction curves for three groups, GS24, GS25, and GS26, with a distinct curve for each group. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionWastewater metagenomic alpha diversity exhibited variation across the three sampling years. Samples were collected in July 2024, June 2025, and March 2026; therefore, sampling year was intrinsically linked to sampling month and season in this study. The composition of sampling sites also varied across years: Hezuo and Zhangye were each represented by two samples in 2024 and 2025, respectively, whereas Dingxi was included only in 2026. Statistical analysis revealed a significant negative correlation between the Simpson index and sampling year, whereas the Shannon index showed a negative but nonsignificant correlation, suggesting that the two diversity metrics captured different aspects of community variation. Overall, the observed changes in alpha diversity may reflect the combined effects of annual, seasonal, and spatial factors. Environmental conditions may have contributed to these between-year differences. Previous research on influent wastewater bacterial communities has demonstrated seasonal structuring associated primarily with wastewater temperature and, in some settings, with precipitation, wastewater flow, and physicochemical variables (LaMartina et al., 2021). These variables should therefore be regarded as plausible confounders of the observed decrease in the present study. Changes in the size, mobility, dietary habits, and infection burden of the contributing population could also plausibly alter the biological inputs into wastewater; however, corresponding demographic data were not available, and their effects could not be evaluated.Technical factors may also have influenced the observed metagenomic profiles. Although clarification and 0.22 μm filtration were used to reduce intact bacterial cells and larger particulate material, filtration alone cannot eliminate extracellular or particle-protected bacterial nucleic acids remaining in a complex wastewater matrix. In addition, the MgCl2-assisted membrane adsorption and elution procedure was used to concentrate virus-containing material but was not a virus-specific affinity-purification step. Most importantly, total nucleic acid was extracted without DNase treatment, allowing residual bacterial DNA and other unprotected DNA to enter the sequencing libraries. These factors likely contributed to the predominance of bacterial reads (>97%) despite viral enrichment, indicating that the procedure concentrated virus-containing wastewater material rather than producing a purified virome. The persistence of bacterial sequences following virion-enrichment procedures has also been reported in sewage metagenomic studies (Cantalupo et al., 2011). Pretreatment with DNase-based enzymes or Benzonase-containing nuclease cocktails before capsid disruption and nucleic acid extraction has been incorporated into virome-preparation workflows to remove non-particle-protected nucleic acids (Cantalupo et al., 2011; Conceicao-Neto et al., 2015; Brinkman et al., 2018). Database-dependent classification represents an additional source of uncertainty because prophage-related sequences and the incomplete representation of environmental microorganisms and viruses in reference databases may affect individual taxonomic assignments (Cantalupo et al., 2011; Roux et al., 2015; Paez-Espino et al., 2016). Furthermore, while the same general experimental workflow was used across the 3 years, unmeasured variation in transport duration, nucleic acid recovery, or sample-processing and sequencing batches could not be separated from sampling year. Kraken2 was unable to classify 56.42–74.74% of the metagenomic reads at the genus level. This unclassified fraction may contain viral sequences that are highly divergent from existing references or poorly represented in current databases—potentially constituting viral “dark matter”—but may also include sequences of nonviral origin and reads containing insufficient information for reliable classification.Among the bacteriophage communities, taxa represented by the family Fiersviridae exhibited high abundance and stability across different time points. As key members of the Fiersviridae family, F-specific RNA phages stably exist in aquatic environments as potential viral indicators of water pollution (Hata et al., 2016). The persistent presence of the families Astroviridae and Picornaviridae (including enteroviruses and kobuviruses) may reflect widespread community shedding. Conversely, the family Reoviridae and the family Hepeviridae consistently remained at extremely low background levels across all temporal cohorts. Because population-level data on virus-specific infection prevalence and vaccination coverage were unavailable, the low relative abundances observed in wastewater could not be reliably attributed to these factors. Furthermore, given the potential detection biases inherent in metagenomic sequencing of complex wastewater samples, these findings should be interpreted cautiously, as the observed low abundances may partly reflect methodological limitations rather than genuinely low viral abundance. Therefore, in future surveillance, supplementary validation combining highly specific targeted enrichment probes or digital PCR technologies may be required for these low-abundance yet high-risk target viruses, to avoid missing potential sporadic sources of infection.The consistently high abundance of plant-associated viruses in wastewater, particularly the genera Tobamovirus and Potexvirus, is not surprising. Previous studies have demonstrated that plant viruses dominate the viral communities in human fecal samples and are widespread across aquatic biomes (Zhang et al., 2006). Specifically, the genus Tobamovirus primarily originates from the daily human consumption of infected plants and their processed products, which pass through the digestive tract and are excreted in large quantities in feces. Although members of the genus Tobamovirus exhibit strict plant-host specificity, a case–control study reported associations between the detection of pepper mild mottle virus in human stool and specific immune responses and clinical symptoms, including fever, abdominal pain, and pruritus; however, causality was not established (Colson et al., 2010; Editors, 2026). Given its exceptionally high environmental abundance and potential relevance to human health, pepper mild mottle virus warrants consideration for inclusion in environmental surveillance systems. Beyond this, pepper mild mottle virus has been widely validated as an ideal environmental indicator for evaluating the viral removal efficacy of wastewater treatment processes, such as conventional activated sludge and membrane bioreactors (Canh et al., 2025). The high relative abundance of members of the genus Potexvirus in this study is noteworthy. Members of this genus primarily infect herbaceous plants, including many economically important crops. Potato virus X, a representative member of the genus and a member of the species Potexvirus ecspotati, is an important pathogen of potato plants (Verchot, 2022). The frequent detection of potexviruses in wastewater may be associated with the agricultural and dietary context of Gansu Province, where potatoes are extensively cultivated and commonly consumed. Viral particles or nucleic acids originating from infected plant materials may enter municipal wastewater through food processing, food-waste disposal, and excretion following consumption. Sewage pipelines frequently harbor substantial insect populations (Cantalupo et al., 2011), which explains the detection of entomopathogenic viral genera such as Alphanodavirus and Betabaculovirus. In nature, these viruses play an ecological role in regulating insect populations, and certain groups, like baculoviruses, have been developed as microbial control agents (Lacey et al., 2015). full_text_sections.other: IntroductionWastewater-based epidemiology has become a prominent approach to noninvasive public health surveillance, offering a comprehensive snapshot of community-level infectious disease dynamics and environmental health (Crits-Christoph et al., 2021). Driven by advances in high-throughput sequencing, the field has successfully transitioned from targeted PCR assays to untargeted, whole-community metagenomic and metatranscriptomic profiling (Tan et al., 2015). Within municipal wastewater, the virome serves as a critical reservoir of biological information, granting real-time insights into the circulating viruses—including human pathogens, bacteriophages, and diverse environmental viruses—thereby acting as a crucial early warning system for emerging infectious diseases (Rothman et al., 2021). Therefore, profiling of the wastewater virome is imperative for comprehensively assessing viral ecological patterns and population health.Gansu Province, located in northwestern China, serves as an ecologically significant region characterized by a distinct arid climate and unique sociogeographical attributes. Although the region’s resident population reached 24.43 million by the end of 2025, Gansu remains a largely unexplored territory in environmental microbiology despite its profound socioenvironmental significance. To bridge this spatial knowledge gap, this study conducted multiyear wastewater sampling across 6 representative cities. Specifically, raw wastewater samples were collected from wastewater treatment plants in Lanzhou, the provincial capital characterized by high population mobility; Hezuo, which has a multiethnic population; Zhangye, an important transportation hub; Jiuquan and Longnan, which border the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Sichuan Province, respectively; and Dingxi, located in central Gansu. The catchment populations served by the sampled wastewater treatment plants exceeded 1 million in Lanzhou and Longnan and 100,000 at each of the other sites. papers.abstract_original: In this study, metagenomic and targeted next-generation sequencing were employed to preliminarily characterize wastewater viral communities in Gansu Province from 2024 to 2026. papers.title_original: High-throughput sequencing reveals the virome characteristics of wastewater in Gansu Province, China from 2024 to 2026

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to characterize the virome of wastewater in Gansu Province, China, from 2024 to 2026, to better understand the presence and diversity of human enteroviruses in this environment. Wastewater-based epidemiology has emerged as a valuable tool for monitoring community disease burden.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved collecting 18 raw wastewater samples from six cities in Gansu Province (Hezuo, Zhangye, Lanzhou, Jiuquan, Longnan, and Dingxi) over three years (2024, 2025, and 2026). The samples were categorized into three groups based on their respective sampling years: GS24, GS25, and GS26.
analysis.methods: Wastewater samples were collected between 2024 and 2026 and processed for metagenomic sequencing. The sequencing depth was sufficient to capture most genus-level diversity, as indicated by rarefaction analysis. The data were analyzed using the Shannon and Simpson indices to assess alpha diversity.
analysis.main_results: The Shannon index showed a negative but nonsignificant correlation with sampling year (Spearman’s ρ = −0.354, p = 0.075), while the Simpson index exhibited a significant negative correlation (Spearman’s ρ = −0.472, p = 0.024). More than 97% of the reads were assigned to Bacteria, with no more than 0.94% classified as viral. Additionally, bacteriophages and plant-infecting viruses showed relatively high abundance and consistent detection patterns.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The significant negative correlation between the Simpson index and sampling year suggests that the diversity metrics captured different aspects of community variation. The study highlights the presence of a complex virome with a notable proportion of viral reads attributed to bacteriophages and plant-associated viruses.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the composition and dynamics of the wastewater virome, which can inform surveillance strategies for human enteroviruses. They also emphasize the importance of considering seasonal and environmental factors in virome studies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by its small number of annual sampling campaigns conducted in different months, which may affect the interpretation of between-year variation. The dataset is considered an exploratory assessment, and the evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the virome characteristics of wastewater in Gansu Province, China, from 2024 to 2026, focusing on human enteroviruses. Six cities were sampled, yielding 18 wastewater samples divided into three groups based on sampling years. High-throughput sequencing revealed that more than 97% of reads were bacterial, with viral reads comprising no more than 0.94%. The Simpson diversity index showed a significant negative correlation with sampling year, while the Shannon index showed a nonsignificant negative trend. Bacteriophages and plant-infecting viruses were relatively abundant and consistently detected. The study highlights the potential of wastewater-based epidemiology for monitoring human enteroviruses but acknowledges limitations due to the limited number of sampling campaigns and the influence of seasonal factors. The evidence is moderate, as the findings are based on exploratory analyses.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在表征 2024 年至 2026 年中国甘肃省废水的病毒组特征,以更好地了解 人肠道病毒 在该环境中的存在和多样性。基于废水的 流行病学 已成为监测社区疾病负担的宝贵工具。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究在三年内(2024年、2025年和2026年)收集了甘肃省六个城市(合作、张掖、兰州、酒泉、陇南和定西)的18个原废水样本。样本根据各自的采样年份分为三组:GS24、GS25 和 GS26。
elements_zh.methods: 2024 年至 2026 年间收集废水样本并进行处理以进行宏基因组测序。如稀疏分析所示,测序深度足以捕获大多数属水平的多样性。使用香农和辛普森指数分析数据以评估阿尔法多样性。
elements_zh.main_results: 香农指数与采样年份呈不显着负相关(Spearman’s ρ = -0.354,p = 0.075),而辛普森指数与采样年份呈显着负相关(Spearman’s ρ = -0.472,p = 0.024)。超过 97% 的读数被归为细菌,不超过 0.94% 被归为病毒。此外,噬菌体和感染植物的病毒表现出相对较高的丰度和一致的检测模式。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 辛普森指数和采样年份之间的显着负相关表明多样性指标捕获了群落变化的不同方面。该研究强调了复杂病毒组的存在,其中很大一部分病毒读数归因于噬菌体和植物相关病毒。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现提供了对废水病毒组的组成和动态的深入了解,这可以为 监测 的 监测 策略提供信息。他们还强调在病毒组研究中考虑季节性和环境因素的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究因其在不同月份进行的年度抽样活动数量较少而受到限制,这可能会影响对年份间变化的解释。该数据集被认为是探索性评估,由于这些限制,证据是中等的。

papers.abstract_zh: 本研究采用宏基因组和靶向下一代测序技术对甘肃省2024年至2026年的废水病毒群落进行了初步表征。总之,本研究提供了甘肃省废水样品中病毒群落特征的初步表征,证明了基于废水的流行病学对人群水平监测的有效性,并强调需要建立结合临床案例监测的协调防御网络关键词: 星状病毒,肠道病毒,甘肃省,宏基因组测序,靶向二代测序,废水 材料与方法 废水样品的采集与处理 2024年至2026年间,从甘肃省6个城市(合作、张掖、兰州、酒泉、陇南、定西)的废水治疗工厂采集了18份原废水样品。为了减少与基于捕获的测序所需的 PCR 循环增加相关的潜在假阳性结果,将初始提取物分为平行和独立的文库制备。使用 ggplot2 包生成稀疏曲线、热图、堆积条形图和 α 多样性指数可视化。病毒组的定量分析为了对病毒群落进行定量分析,使用公式 1 中描述的每百万读数归一化方法估计相对丰度。摘要新出现和重新出现的传染病继续对全球公共卫生安全构成持续挑战。作为一种公正且非侵入性的人群层面的 监测 方法,基于废水的 监测 已成为一种城市规模的监测工具,用于主动捕获社区疾病状况。

news.title: Enterovirus D68 - Sada Elbalad English

news.content: Follow us Sada Elbalad Group Egypt Middle East World Business Tourism Culture & heritage Lifestyle More entertainment Sports Science & Tech opinion In depth Videos & Features Photo Gallery Supervisor Elham AbolFateh Editor-in-chief Mohamed Wadie Home / opinion OPINION Add as Preferred Source Written by Dr Magdy Badran Fri 09 Oct 2026 | 11:57 PM · 5 min read Enterovirus D68 Share this column Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is an emerging respiratory pathogen belonging to the family Picornaviridae and the genus Enterovirus. First identified in California in 1962, it was initially reported infrequently. However, major outbreaks, particularly in 2014, established EV-D68 as an important cause of respiratory illness, especially among children. Unlike many enteroviruses associated with gastrointestinal or neurological diseases, EV-D68 primarily affects the respiratory tract. Infection may cause mild cold-like symptoms, but some patients develop severe respiratory distress, particularly children with asthma or other underlying respiratory conditions. EV-D68 has also been associated with acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a rare neurological syndrome that can cause sudden weakness in the arms or legs. Routes of Spread EV-D68 spreads primarily through respiratory secretions and close interpersonal contact. Important transmission routes include: • Respiratory droplets: Secretions released during coughing and sneezing can expose people nearby. • Direct contact: Contact with nasal mucus or saliva from an infected person may transfer the virus. • Contaminated hands and surfaces: Touching contaminated objects and subsequently touching the eyes, nose, or mouth may contribute to transmission. • Close-contact environments: Homes, schools, childcare facilities, and healthcare settings may facilitate spread when preventive measures are inadequate. People with mild symptoms or no noticeable symptoms may contribute to transmission, making case identification difficult. The relative contribution of different transmission routes is not fully established, and EV-D68 should not be assumed to spread in exactly the same way as every other enterovirus. Strains and Genetic Diversity EV-D68 is genetically diverse, with major clades A, B, C, and D identified through molecular classification, primarily using the VP1 gene. Clade B, including subclades B1, B2, and B3, has been prominent in several outbreaks, while clade distribution varies geographically and over time. Prevalence and Global Distribution EV-D68 occurs internationally, but its true prevalence is difficult to determine. Many infections are mild or asymptomatic, and routine respiratory testing may not distinguish EV-D68 from other enteroviruses or rhinoviruses. Consequently, reported laboratory detections represent only part of the total burden of infection. Exposure to EV-D68 is widespread. Antibodies against the virus increase with age, and some study populations have approached 100% seropositivity by approximately 20 years of age. However, seropositivity indicates previous immune recognition; it does not establish the number of current infections or guarantee complete protection. In temperate climates, EV-D68 activity often increases during summer and autumn, although infections can occur throughout the year. The timing of peaks varies geographically. Symptoms and Clinical Presentation The severity of EV-D68 infection varies considerably. Mild symptoms include: • Runny or blocked nose. • Sneezing and cough. • Sore throat. • Muscle and body aches. • Fever, which may be absent. More serious respiratory manifestations include: • Wheezing and worsening asthma. • Rapid or labored breathing. • Lower respiratory tract infection. • Pneumonia and, in severe cases, respiratory failure. Infants, children, and adolescents are important affected groups because they may have less prior immunity. Children with asthma or other underlying medical conditions may face a greater risk of severe respiratory illness. Nevertheless, severe infection is possible in people without known chronic disease. Complications EV-D68 is important because it can increase pediatric hospital admissions, strain respiratory care services, and cause serious complications. One of the most concerning complications is acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a rare neurological syndrome involving spinal cord gray matter. It can cause sudden weakness in one or more limbs, reduced muscle tone and reflexes, pain, swallowing difficulties, facial weakness, or slurred speech. Neurological symptoms may develop after a respiratory illness rather than at the same time. EV-D68 has been strongly associated with AFM, but most infected individuals do not develop it, and not every AFM case is caused by EV-D68. The broader public health priorities are early recognition, outbreak investigation, molecular surveillance, protection of children with asthma, and prompt evaluation of respiratory distress or sudden limb weakness. COVID-19's Impact on Enterovirus D68 The COVID-19 pandemic severely disrupted the natural transmission and biennial seasonal cycles of Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) globally. During the height of the pandemic, public health measures like social distancing and mask mandates successfully suppressed the virus, causing case counts and genetic diversity to drop to historic lows. However, this prolonged lack of exposure created a significant "immunity gap" in the pediatric population. When pandemic restrictions were lifted, the virus rebounded sharply, causing atypical, out-of-season resurgences that shifted traditional biennial timelines and triggered widespread respiratory illness in children. Additionally, these post-pandemic changes heavily altered the predictability of Acute Flaccid Myelitis (AFM). Why Is There No Vaccine Against EV-D68? Developing an EV-D68 vaccine faces scientific and practical challenges, but vaccination remains a potential future strategy. Genetic diversity: Multiple viral clades complicate the development of vaccines that provide broad, durable protection. Uncertain protective immunity: Researchers still need to establish which immune responses prevent infection, severe respiratory disease, and neurological complications. Clinical trial challenges: Severe complications are uncommon, and unpredictable seasonal outbreaks make vaccine efficacy studies difficult and costly. Research and funding: Sustained investment is needed to develop, test, and manufacture effective vaccines. Continued research into vaccine candidates and protective immunity is essential. Prevention No specific vaccine is currently available to prevent EV-D68 infection. Prevention therefore depends on reducing exposure and recognizing illness early. Recommended measures include: 1. Hand hygiene: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water, particularly after coughing, sneezing, or wiping the nose. 2. Respiratory hygiene: Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or the elbow and dispose of used tissues safely. 3. Surface cleaning: Regularly clean frequently touched objects, toys, and shared surfaces using appropriate products. 4. Reducing exposure: Avoid close contact with people who are ill, and stay home when sick when feasible. 5. Healthcare precautions: Apply appropriate standard, contact, and droplet precautions according to clinical infection-control guidance. 6. Asthma management: Ensure that children with asthma follow their prescribed treatment plans and have access to appropriate rescue medication. Difficulty breathing requires urgent medical assessment. Sudden weakness of an arm or leg, difficulty swallowing, or facial weakness also requires immediate evaluation. #Enterovirus D68 Dr Magdy Badran Contributor at SEE News — Sada Elbalad English. Conditions EV-D68 Reaches Some of the Highest Wastewater Levels Since Tracking Began, Raising Concern for Children with Asthma Published Oct 07, 2026 11:10 PM EDT By Cole Mercer iStock | Anastasia Dobrusina Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket Enterovirus D68, a respiratory virus that can set off serious breathing problems in children with asthma, was found in about 72% of U.S. wastewater samples in September, up from about 20% in August, according to WastewaterSCAN. The program said that "since mid-September 2026, we are seeing some of the highest concentrations of EV-D68 we've measured since monitoring began back in September 2023," and it placed the virus in its high category nationally. Wastewater shows that a virus is spreading in a community. It does not count sick people, and it cannot predict how many children will need care. Still, the signal arrives as children crowd back into classrooms, and families of kids with asthma have the most reason to prepare. The main concern is breathing. A much rarer complication, acute flaccid myelitis, or AFM, can cause sudden limb weakness and needs emergency care, but it remains uncommon. Rising Levels in California and Other Regions WastewaterSCAN reported more positive EV-D68 detections across the Midwest, Northeast and South. It said activity in the West was lower than in other regions. Even so, edhat reported high levels in San Jose, Palo Alto, Redwood City and San Francisco, with detections in Sacramento, Santa Rosa, Santa Cruz, Vallejo and other Northern California communities. EV-D68 usually circulates in late summer and early fall, with major outbreaks often occurring every other year. WastewaterSCAN recorded a large wave across all four U.S. regions in 2024. Because wastewater captures virus shed by people with and without symptoms, it can signal rising spread before clinics see a jump in visits. MedicalDaily previously reported that sudden arm or leg weakness in a child is an emergency, focusing on AFM warning signs. The new wastewater data shift the practical question toward day-to-day asthma care, since breathing problems are the far more common result of infection. Breathing Trouble and the Rare Risk of Limb Weakness According to the CDC, mild EV-D68 symptoms may include runny nose, sneezing, cough, and muscle aches. More severe illness can bring wheezing, difficulty breathing, or pneumonia. "Children with asthma may be at higher risk for severe symptoms from EV-D68 and other respiratory illnesses," the agency says. There is no vaccine and no specific antiviral treatment. AFM is a rare but serious condition that affects the spinal cord and can cause muscle weakness, sometimes leading to permanent paralysis. As of September 3, the CDC had confirmed 10 AFM cases in 2026 and 17 in 2025, and 800 since tracking began in 2014. Peak years brought 120 cases in 2014, 153 in 2016, and 238 in 2018. The link between EV-D68 waves and AFM has weakened lately. A July 2026 CDC surveillance report noted that recent EV-D68 strains lack some genetic changes tied to nerve damage in mouse and nerve cell models. That is an explanation still under study, not a guarantee, and doctors still treat any sudden limb weakness as an emergency. Steps Parents of Children with Asthma Can Take Now The most useful step is reviewing your child's asthma action plan, the written guide that sorts symptoms into green, yellow, and red zones. The CDC says, "Everyone with asthma needs their own Asthma Action Plan," created with a health care provider. If the plan is out of date or your child's medicines have changed, ask the pediatrician to update it. Make sure controller and rescue inhalers are filled and not expired, and that the school nurse has a current copy of the plan. The CDC also recommends that people with asthma take prescribed medicines as directed and get a yearly flu shot. Regular handwashing and keeping sick children home help reduce spread. Call a doctor if cold symptoms worsen or rescue medicine is needed more often than the action plan allows. Seek emergency care for trouble breathing that does not improve with rescue medicine, or for any sudden weakness of an arm or leg, facial droop, or difficulty swallowing. WastewaterSCAN publishes monthly updates, and the CDC updates AFM counts through the season. For most families, the right response is preparation, not alarm. Most children with EV-D68 have a mild, cold-like illness. Read more Your Mom's Exposure To Smoke May Have Caused Your Asthma 82% Of US Adults Favor Smoking Ban In Cars When Children Present; Kids More Likely To Start Smoking From Secondhand Exposure CDC Model Now Puts COVID Growth in 35 States, Down from 48, While Rhinovirus and Strep Climb Key Questions Answered What is EV-D68? It is an enterovirus that usually causes cold-like illness but can cause severe breathing problems, especially in children with asthma. How widespread is it now? WastewaterSCAN detected it in about 72% of U.S. samples in September, up from about 20% in August. Is there a vaccine or treatment? No. There is no vaccine and no specific antiviral. Care focuses on symptoms and breathing support. How common is AFM? It is rare. The CDC confirmed 10 cases in 2026 as of September 3. When should I seek emergency care? Go for trouble breathing that does not improve with rescue medicine, or any sudden arm or leg weakness, facial droop, or trouble swallowing. More severe illness can bring wheezing, difficulty breathing, or pneumonia. "Children with asthma may be at higher risk for severe symptoms from EV-D68 and other respiratory illnesses," the agency says. There is no vaccine and no specific antiviral treatment. AFM is a rare but serious condition that affects the spinal cord and can cause muscle weakness, sometimes leading to permanent paralysis. As of September 3, the CDC had confirmed 10 AFM cases in 2026 and 17 in 2025, and 800 since tracking began in 2014. Peak years brought 120 cases in 2014, 153 in 2016, and 238 in 2018. The link between EV-D68 waves and AFM has weakened lately. A July 2026 CDC surveillance report noted that recent EV-D68 strains lack some genetic changes tied to nerve damage in mouse and nerve cell models. That is an explanation still under study, not a guarantee, and doctors still treat any sudden limb weakness as an emergency. Steps Parents of Children with Asthma Can Take Now The most useful step is reviewing your child's asthma action plan, the written guide that sorts symptoms into green, yellow, and red zones. The CDC says, "Everyone with asthma needs their own Asthma Action Plan," created with a health care provider. If the plan is out of date or your child's medicines have changed, ask the pediatrician to update it. Make sure controller and rescue inhalers are filled and not expired, and that the school nurse has a current copy of the plan. The CDC also recommends that people with asthma take prescribed medicines as directed and get a yearly flu shot. Regular handwashing and keeping sick children home help reduce spread. Call a doctor if cold symptoms worsen or rescue medicine is needed more often than the action plan allows. Seek emergency care for trouble breathing that does not improve with rescue medicine, or for any sudden weakness of an arm or leg, facial droop, or difficulty swallowing. WastewaterSCAN publishes monthly updates, and the CDC updates AFM counts through the season. For most families, the right response is preparation, not alarm. Most children with EV-D68 have a mild, cold-like illness. It is an enterovirus that usually causes cold-like illness but can cause severe breathing problems, especially in children with asthma. How widespread is it now? WastewaterSCAN detected it in about 72% of U.S. samples in September, up from about 20% in August. Is there a vaccine or treatment? No. There is no vaccine and no specific antiviral. Care focuses on symptoms and breathing support. How common is AFM? It is rare. The CDC confirmed 10 cases in 2026 as of September 3. When should I seek emergency care? analysis.brief_en: The EV-D68 virus is spreading in parts of California, according to reports. This enterovirus, which causes respiratory illness with symptoms similar to a common cold, has been detected in wastewater surveillance in areas including Palo Alto, Napa, southeastern San Francisco, and San Rafael. Health experts warn that children may be particularly vulnerable to severe illness, including breathing difficulties or pneumonia. In rare cases, EV-D68 can lead to acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a serious neurological condition. Parents are advised to seek immediate medical attention if children show unusual symptoms. The spread of EV-D68 is being monitored by WastewaterSCAN, a community wastewater monitoring system. The virus is not classified as a polio virus, but its potential to cause a polio-like illness raises concerns. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has noted that EV-D68 can lead to severe complications in children, emphasizing the need for vigilance and prompt medical intervention.

For decades, clinicians have struggled to explain why two children infected with the same enterovirus can experience such dramatically different outcomes. A new candidate-gene association study from China now adds a piece to that puzzle, examining whether inherited variation in genes that govern the complement system, a key arm of innate immunity, influences the severity of disease caused by Coxsackievirus A6. The study, published in Virology Journal by Ying Li of Zhengzhou Railway Vocational and Technical College and colleagues at Zhengzhou University and Henan Children’s Hospital, focused on children of Han Chinese ethnicity who were infected with Coxsackievirus A6, an enterovirus that has increasingly displaced enterovirus 71 as the dominant cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease outbreaks in many regions. The research team enrolled 189 children from Henan Children’s Hospital, dividing them into 94 severe cases and 95 mild cases, and then asked whether specific single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs, in complement-related genes were more common among the severely ill children than among those with milder disease. The complement system is a cascade of plasma proteins that acts as one of the body’s first lines of defense against pathogens. When activated, complement proteins such as C3 and C5 mark microbes for destruction, recruit inflammatory cells to sites of infection, and in some circumstances directly punch holes in viral envelopes or infected cell membranes. Because the complement cascade sits at the interface between pathogen recognition and inflammatory damage, it represents a biologically plausible target for genetic studies of infection severity: too little complement activity might impair viral clearance, while too much might fuel the excessive inflammation that characterizes severe cases. The central complement protein C3, the terminal component C5, and the complement regulatory protein factor H, encoded by the CFH gene, each play distinct roles in this delicate balance, and common genetic variants in these genes have previously been linked to susceptibility to other infectious and inflammatory diseases. To test whether such variants matter in Coxsackievirus A6 infection, the researchers extracted genomic DNA from peripheral blood leukocytes using a modified phenol-chloroform method and performed SNP genotyping by polymerase chain reaction followed by restriction fragment length polymorphism analysis, a classical technique in which PCR-amplified DNA fragments are digested with restriction enzymes whose cutting patterns differ depending on the nucleotide present at a given position. This approach allowed the team to determine each child’s genotype at candidate SNPs in the C5, C3, and CFH genes and to compare genotype frequencies between severe and mild cases using both crude and multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for age group and sex. The results revealed several nominal associations. Children carrying the GA genotype at rs3761847 in the C5 gene had roughly two and a half times the odds of severe disease compared with those carrying the GG genotype, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.523 and a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 1.036 to 6.143. At rs2250656 in the C3 gene, the TC genotype was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.982, with a confidence interval of 1.061 to 3.704, relative to the TT genotype. The strongest signals emerged at rs1065489 in the CFH gene, where the TT genotype conferred an adjusted odds ratio of 3.125, with a confidence interval of 1.249 to 7.818, and the GT genotype an adjusted odds ratio of 2.499, with a confidence interval of 1.118 to 5.588, both relative to the GG genotype. Taken at face value, these findings suggest that children carrying particular alleles at these three loci face a substantially elevated risk of progressing to severe hand, foot, and mouth disease once infected with Coxsackievirus A6. However, the authors are careful to emphasize a critical statistical caveat. When the analysis was corrected for multiple testing using the Bonferroni method, a conservative procedure that adjusts the significance threshold to account for the number of SNPs examined, none of these associations remained statistically significant. This is a common and important pattern in candidate-gene association studies, which typically examine a modest number of preselected variants in a limited number of participants. Nominal signals that vanish after correction may reflect true effects that the study lacked the statistical power to confirm, or they may simply be chance findings that arise whenever many genetic variants are tested simultaneously in a finite sample. Distinguishing between these possibilities requires replication in independent cohorts, which is precisely what the authors call for. Beyond the individual SNP analyses, the team also evaluated whether a combined model incorporating multiple SNPs could discriminate severe from mild cases. The combined model showed limited discriminatory performance, achieving an apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.653, which declined to 0.631 after bootstrap-based optimism correction. An AUC of 0.5 indicates discrimination no better than chance, while 1.0 indicates perfect discrimination, so a corrected value of 0.631 suggests that complement-related variants alone, at least in this cohort, provide only modest predictive information about disease severity. This finding underscores a broader lesson in genetic epidemiology: complex clinical outcomes such as infection severity are rarely determined by a handful of variants in a single pathway, and even biologically plausible genetic associations often translate into weak predictive models when considered in isolation. The study also reported exploratory differences in selected laboratory parameters across genotype groups, hinting that complement variants might correlate with measurable differences in the host response to infection, although the authors frame these observations as preliminary. Such genotype-phenotype correlations, if confirmed, could eventually help explain the biological mechanism linking specific variants to clinical outcomes, for example by altering complement protein levels, activation efficiency, or regulation of the inflammatory response during enterovirus infection. The clinical context of this work is significant. Coxsackievirus A6 has emerged as a major cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease in China and elsewhere, and unlike enterovirus 71, for which vaccines have been developed and deployed, CVA6 has no licensed vaccine. Surveillance data have shown shifting patterns of enterovirus dominance, with CVA6 outbreaks producing atypical and sometimes severe presentations, including widespread eczema coxsackium in children with atopic dermatitis and occasional neurological involvement. Understanding the host-side determinants of severity therefore has practical value: if genetic risk factors could be reliably identified and validated, they might eventually inform risk stratification in clinical settings, helping clinicians identify which children warrant closer monitoring during outbreaks. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Life Sciences Institutional Review Board of Zhengzhou University, with written informed consent obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all participants. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and several provincial and postdoctoral programs, the work exemplifies the growing effort to move beyond purely virological explanations of disease severity and toward an integrated view in which viral factors, host genetics, and immune status jointly shape clinical outcomes. For now, the message of this study is one of cautious hypothesis generation: complement-related variants in C5, C3, and CFH merit further investigation as potential modifiers of Coxsackievirus A6 disease severity, but larger, independent, and ideally multi-center cohorts will be needed before these genetic signals can be considered established or translated into clinical tools. In a field where most children recover uneventfully and only a minority deteriorate, even modest advances in understanding host susceptibility could ultimately sharpen the clinical response to one of the world’s most burdensome pediatric viral diseases. Children carrying the GA genotype at rs3761847 in the C5 gene had roughly two and a half times the odds of severe disease compared with those carrying the GG genotype, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.523 and a 95 percent confidence interval spanning 1.036 to 6.143. At rs2250656 in the C3 gene, the TC genotype was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.982, with a confidence interval of 1.061 to 3.704, relative to the TT genotype. The strongest signals emerged at rs1065489 in the CFH gene, where the TT genotype conferred an adjusted odds ratio of 3.125, with a confidence interval of 1.249 to 7.818, and the GT genotype an adjusted odds ratio of 2.499, with a confidence interval of 1.118 to 5.588, both relative to the GG genotype. Taken at face value, these findings suggest that children carrying particular alleles at these three loci face a substantially elevated risk of progressing to severe hand, foot, and mouth disease once infected with Coxsackievirus A6. However, the authors are careful to emphasize a critical statistical caveat. When the analysis was corrected for multiple testing using the Bonferroni method, a conservative procedure that adjusts the significance threshold to account for the number of SNPs examined, none of these associations remained statistically significant. This is a common and important pattern in candidate-gene association studies, which typically examine a modest number of preselected variants in a limited number of participants. Nominal signals that vanish after correction may reflect true effects that the study lacked the statistical power to confirm, or they may simply be chance findings that arise whenever many genetic variants are tested simultaneously in a finite sample. Distinguishing between these possibilities requires replication in independent cohorts, which is precisely what the authors call for. Beyond the individual SNP analyses, the team also evaluated whether a combined model incorporating multiple SNPs could discriminate severe from mild cases. The combined model showed limited discriminatory performance, achieving an apparent area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.653, which declined to 0.631 after bootstrap-based optimism correction. An AUC of 0.5 indicates discrimination no better than chance, while 1.0 indicates perfect discrimination, so a corrected value of 0.631 suggests that complement-related variants alone, at least in this cohort, provide only modest predictive information about disease severity. This finding underscores a broader lesson in genetic epidemiology: complex clinical outcomes such as infection severity are rarely determined by a handful of variants in a single pathway, and even biologically plausible genetic associations often translate into weak predictive models when considered in isolation. The study also reported exploratory differences in selected laboratory parameters across genotype groups, hinting that complement variants might correlate with measurable differences in the host response to infection, although the authors frame these observations as preliminary. Such genotype-phenotype correlations, if confirmed, could eventually help explain the biological mechanism linking specific variants to clinical outcomes, for example by altering complement protein levels, activation efficiency, or regulation of the inflammatory response during enterovirus infection. The clinical context of this work is significant. Coxsackievirus A6 has emerged as a major cause of hand, foot, and mouth disease in China and elsewhere, and unlike enterovirus 71, for which vaccines have been developed and deployed, CVA6 has no licensed vaccine. Surveillance data have shown shifting patterns of enterovirus dominance, with CVA6 outbreaks producing atypical and sometimes severe presentations, including widespread eczema coxsackium in children with atopic dermatitis and occasional neurological involvement. Understanding the host-side determinants of severity therefore has practical value: if genetic risk factors could be reliably identified and validated, they might eventually inform risk stratification in clinical settings, helping clinicians identify which children warrant closer monitoring during outbreaks. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Life Sciences Institutional Review Board of Zhengzhou University, with written informed consent obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all participants. Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and several provincial and postdoctoral programs, the work exemplifies the growing effort to move beyond purely virological explanations of disease severity and toward an integrated view in which viral factors, host genetics, and immune status jointly shape clinical outcomes. For now, the message of this study is one of cautious hypothesis generation: complement-related variants in C5, C3, and CFH merit further investigation as potential modifiers of Coxsackievirus A6 disease severity, but larger, independent, and ideally multi-center cohorts will be needed before these genetic signals can be considered established or translated into clinical tools. In a field where most children recover uneventfully and only a minority deteriorate, even modest advances in understanding host susceptibility could ultimately sharpen the clinical response to one of the world’s most burdensome pediatric viral diseases. Detection levels are described as high and continuing to climb in Palo Alto, Napa, southeast San Francisco and San Rafael, according to the virus's typical late-summer-to-early-fall pattern. The local uptick tracks a much larger national surge. As reported by The Independent, wastewater monitoring network WastewaterSCAN, which tracks traces of viruses in municipal sewage, found the virus in roughly 72% of national samples collected in September, a jump from just 20% in August, according to an October 2 update reported by Bay Area Telegraph. That spike pushed the pathogen to a “high” national classification, giving Bay Area families a clearer sense of just how widespread the current wave has become. Enterovirus D68 is one of more than 100 non-polio enteroviruses circulating in the United States, and for most people it causes a cold-like illness — cough, shortness of breath and wheezing. Children infected with the virus may develop fever, difficulty breathing or pneumonia, according to the CDC. Infants, children and teenagers can be more seriously affected because they may lack immunity built up from previous exposure to the virus. A Rare but Serious Complication The condition drawing the most concern is acute flaccid myelitis, or AFM — an uncommon but dangerous neurological condition that mainly affects children. Symptoms typically appear several weeks after an enterovirus D68 infection and can include arm or leg weakness, loss of muscle tone and reflexes, pain, difficulty swallowing, slurred speech, difficulty moving the eyes, or facial droop or weakness. The virus isn't new to California. It was first isolated by public health researchers in the state back in 1962, remaining an infrequently detected pathogen for decades before evolving into the larger outbreak strains that began appearing in the 2010s, per SFGATE. The first major U.S. epidemic hit in 2014, when federal public health laboratories confirmed 1,116 cases of severe respiratory illness across 47 states and Washington, D.C., with many hospitalized children requiring mechanical ventilation, according to the CDC. Despite that history, AFM itself has remained rare. Since standardized national tracking began in August 2014, the CDC has recorded 800 confirmed AFM cases nationwide as of September 3, 2026, with peak years in 2014, 2016 and 2018. Over 90% of reported AFM cases occur in young children, with a historical median age of onset between 4 and 7 years old — one reason pediatricians and parents of young kids remain the primary audience for public health warnings on this virus. Why Case Counts Don't Tell the Whole Story Enterovirus D68 itself is not a nationally reportable disease, meaning local and state health departments aren't required to track routine clinical cases or deaths tied to it. That's part of why wastewater data, rather than emergency room counts, has become the primary early warning tool for tracking its spread. Suspected AFM cases are treated differently: public health regulations across states and territories require providers to immediately report any suspected Patients Under Investigation for the condition to local health departments, per CDC guidance. The California Department of Public Health issued a health advisory this past July reminding clinicians to stay alert for EV-D68 respiratory illness and potential AFM cases during the late-summer and early-fall window, while recommending poliovirus stool testing to rule out other paralytic causes, according to Napa County health alerts. Notably, CDC epidemiological data from 2020 through 2025 show annual AFM cases have stayed low, between 17 and 48 per year, even during substantial EV-D68 respiratory surges in 2022 and 2024 — leaving researchers still investigating why recent circulating strains haven't translated into more neurological complications. Older adults, small children and immunocompromised people are considered at greatest risk of severe illness from the virus. Dr. Monica Gandhi said respiratory illnesses can be severe for certain risk groups, underscoring why vigilance matters even as overall AFM numbers stay low. Asthma and Other Risk Factors One group deserves particular attention: kids with asthma. A CDC-led multicenter study published in JAMA Network Open found that among children hospitalized with EV-D68 respiratory illness, 37.1% had a pre-existing diagnosis of asthma or reactive airway disease, according to CIDRAP. That makes early medical evaluation especially important for families with asthmatic children during this surge. There's no vaccine for enterovirus D68. The most effective protections remain familiar ones: frequently washing hands and avoiding contact with sick people. Bay Area residents are also being encouraged to get updated flu shots and COVID-19 vaccines this fall. The timing adds urgency. The San Francisco Department of Public Health announced the city's first flu-related death of the season on October 1. Dr. Susan Philip said respiratory viruses such as flu and COVID should be taken very seriously, especially for people at higher risk of getting sick, adding that vaccines help people stay healthy and participate in fall festivities.
